analysis.one_liner: Restores patients' right to sue medical device makers in state courts for faulty devices.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 110 cosponsors and got a subcommittee hearing, but never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2008 the Supreme Court ruled that federal approval of a medical device blocks patients from suing the manufacturer under state law when the device injures them. H.R. 1346 would have overturned that shield, amending federal device law to say it does not affect anyone's liability under state law, and it would have applied to lawsuits already in progress. The bill never came to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients injured by FDA-cleared or FDA-approved medical devices, and their families, who under current law cannot collect damages from the manufacturer in state court because federal approval preempts their claims. The bill would have let those lawsuits proceed, including cases already filed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients hurt by faulty medical devices

how_it_helps.text: Adds a provision to federal device law stating that nothing in the preemption section modifies or affects any action for damages or any person's liability under state law.
Makes the change take effect as if it had been part of the original 1976 Medical Device Amendments, and applies it to any civil action pending or filed after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Medical device manufacturers, which would face damages lawsuits in state courts for devices they sell with federal approval, including litigation over devices already on the market. Some of that cost would flow to prices and to settlement payments.

drawbacks.text: Device makers and their allies argued that allowing state juries to second-guess FDA-reviewed devices would expose companies to inconsistent verdicts and add litigation costs, which some predicted would be passed on in device prices and could discourage innovation.
Because the bill applied retroactively to pending cases, it would have changed the legal rules midstream for lawsuits already in the courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: a patient permanently injured by a defective device that the FDA approved currently has no state-law remedy. The main cost is higher liability exposure for device makers, some of which would reach patients through prices. A reasonable trade-off question is whether juries should be able to second-guess FDA determinations, but for people catastrophically injured by a device, the bill offered the only compensation path available.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee — which held one hearing — and never got a markup or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 5, 2009 with 64 original cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
It was referred to the Health Subcommittee on March 6, 2009, which held a hearing on May 12, 2009.
It attracted 110 cosponsors — 102 of 253 House Democrats and 8 of 178 House Republicans.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical device manufacturers are better off because the bill died: the 2008 Supreme Court preemption shield remains in place, so they still cannot be sued in state court over FDA-approved devices, even by patients already in litigation.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 110 cosponsors, including both parties.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee through one Health Subcommittee hearing on May 12, 2009; never reported it out for a floor vote.

against.name: Medical device industry
against.role: Device manufacturers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and lobbied against reopening state-court liability for FDA-approved devices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and drew 110 cosponsors split 102 Democrats and 8 Republicans, but with no recorded vote there is no breakdown of how the parties would have voted on passage.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped away the 2008 Supreme Court ruling that federal device approval blocks state-law damages suits, exposing makers to lawsuits from injured patients, including cases already pending. The industry's interest in the bill ran against the people it injures, whose current legal remedy is limited to narrow federal channels.

Reopening state-court claims for device injuries would create a new pool of cases for attorneys representing injured patients. Their interest runs alongside patients', though they profit from the same lawsuits.
